bibliography.abstract: Focusing on the two linear developments at the forefront of 21st-century urbanism, the High Line in New York City and the Line in Saudi Arabia, the article argues that both create ruptures, albeit very differently: in the first case in the urban fabric and in the second case in the landscape – the first reuses and retains existing urban infrastructure while the second ruptures the desert environment with a massive investment in infrastructure with purportedly sustainable tools. The High Line and the Line embody the kind of rupture in which seemingly sustainable efforts reorder and re-ruin spaces to make them either actively exclusionary in the case of the Line, or to struggle, and at times achieve, bridges for social connectedness, as is happening with the High Line. The “second face‘ of the High Line is suggestive of the potential to mend the ruptures and reshape social practices in its public space through inventive design interventions. The article draws on Richard Sennett, Saskia Sassen, and Susan Fainstein to consider these developments through conceptualizations of urban disorder, the theoretical lenses of global urbanism and the ’just city,” and offers insight into the limitations and possibilities for resistance in contemporary planetary urbanism.

en.caveats: The study is entirely theoretical and conceptual, relying on qualitative literature and urban theory rather than empirical spatial data or field measurements.
en.what: This paper presents a comparative theoretical analysis of two prominent 21st-century linear urban developments: the High Line in New York City and the Line in Saudi Arabia. It examines how the High Line repurposes existing infrastructure to create ruptures in the urban fabric while striving for social connectedness, whereas the Line ruptures the desert landscape through a massive, exclusionary infrastructural investment. The analysis applies theories of urban disorder, global urbanism, and the 'just city' to evaluate both projects.
en.why: It establishes a conceptual framework for understanding how linear urban forms can simultaneously act as forces of spatial rupture and as potential sites for social mending and public resistance.
